newsitem.title: UK: Supply gap to push gold price to $580 by 2010 - EIU.
newsitem.headline: Supply gap to push gold price to $580 by 2010 - EIU.

text.p: A supply gap too great to be filled by central bank sales and Far Eastern investor liquidation will push gold prices to $580 per ounce by 2010, the Economic Intelligence Unit (EIU) said in a report.
"The EIU forcasts that the real price of gold, measured in 1995 U.S. dollars, will increase by almost three percent per year over the forecast period," its report, Gold to 2010, said.
The price would rise gradually, achieving $440 by the new millennium and $490 by 2005, it added.
"Speculators, however, may be disappointed; the supply shortfall is unlikely to be dramatic," the report said.
The EIU said its price forecast was the most likely of three scenarios, pegged with a 60 percent probability.

Another more bullish scenario, in which gold rises to $558 by 2000 and $860 by 2010, was given a 25 percent chance of occuring, while the third outlook, with only 15 percent probability, saw prices rising to $448 by 2000 and $462 by 2010.
Key to the price scenario is the view that Far East demand will continue to grow and that central bank sales will be well managed and aimed at not destabilising the market.

"After 2000 the gold price will have more to do with inflation rates in the Far East than in other parts of the world. With higher growth rates, Asia-Pacific inflation will be accelerating and this could well give the price an added boost," the EIU report said.
Overall demand is expected to rise from 16,435 tonnes in 1991-1995 to 17,417 tonnes in 1996-2000 before stabilising at 17,298 tonnes in 2005-2010.
At the same time supply is declining, with South African resources running deeper and costs climbing.

"Currently it would take a price of at least $500 per ounce to make it worthwhile to mine the bulk of South Africa's remaining gold and costs are rising so fast in many mines that within a decade $600 per ounce (at 1995 prices) would be needed," it added.
There are 18,700 tonnes of proven gold reserves in the world that can be mined at current prices, but only 8,000-8,500 tonnes will be available to the market over the next 15 years, it said.

"Most of Russia's reserves, for instance, which account for nearly one quarter of this store, will be unavailable because of the political risk and organisational problems faced by the country," the report said.
Adding 5,000 tonnes of possible central bank sales brings the total to 13,500-14,000 tonnes, barely enough to cover four years of current physical demand less recycled gold.
"Clearly the market is relying heavily on the souk and bar hoarders to disgorge significant amounts to gold. But will they do so at current prices?" the report asked.
"All the evidence suggests that they will not. In which case something else will have to give, and we believe it will be the price," it said.
